written_by: Darby, award-level creative and UX pass 2026-10-04 evening (earlier version by worker e4475a)
person_made_it: A person who read Saute's four-step flow, hated the dead first step, and drew one board where the food and the price sit next to each other; the pictograms and the receipt tape are drawn by hand, not pulled from a kit.
emcee_who_is_speaking: A kitchen host, plain and warm, who says Sunday, Downey, and the price, and does not claim to be Fina or tell her story, because she has not told it to us yet.
what_time_of_day_is_this_room: Thursday night on a phone, an hour before the board closes; the countdown and the Sunday date are the first numbers on the screen.
did_the_click_pay_me: Yes: one tap adds a dish, the tape prints it, the thermometer moves, and at 5, 10 and 15 the price of every meal in the bag drops in view. On desktop the twelve numbered dish cells under the name jump straight to each tile.
works_for_the_recipient: Fina and Brian can swap the sample prices and the address in one file; eaters can order with JavaScript off; Gordon can judge it against sautemeals.co side by side, category by category.
taught_me_something: The price ladder was always the upsell; Saute hid it in a FAQ sentence, and showing it as a thermometer turned a rule into a reason to add two more.
told_me_the_truth: The desktop line used to read 'Meal Kitchen, . Come hungry Sunday.' because a CSS rule hid the city; it now says Downey, California. Prices, Sunday windows and ZIP bands stay labeled sample; every dish photo, including the five added tonight, is labeled illustrative.
weakest: All twelve tiles now have photos, but they are illustrative, not Fina's plates; the Greek Chicken photo shows a yogurt sauce the allergen row does not mention because allergens come only from dish names. Real prices, address and hours are still missing, and the desktop first add control still sits below the first screen.
